Very good morning. The 10,223rd meeting of the Security Council is called to order. The provisional agenda for this meeting is the situation in Afghanistan. The agenda is adopted. In accordance with rule 37 of the Council's provisional rules of procedure, I invite the representatives of Afghanistan, India, Kazakhstan, and the Islamic Republic of Iran to participate in this meeting. It is so decided. In accordance with rule 39 of the Council's provisional rules of procedure, I invite the following briefers to participate in this meeting: Ms. Georgette Gagnon, Deputy Special Representative for Afghanistan and Officer-in-Charge of UNAMA; and Ms. Najis Nehan, Founder and Executive Director of Farajiyah. It is so decided. The Security Council will now begin its consideration of item 2 of the agenda. I wish to draw the attention of Council members to the Secretary-General's report on the situation in Afghanistan and its implications for international peace and security, document reference S/2026/724. I would like to welcome Ms. Gagnon, who is in Kabul. I give her the floor. You have the floor, Ms. Gagnon.

Mr. President, last month, The de facto authorities marked the fifth year of their return to power. They projected confidence, highlighting nationwide control, improved security, infrastructure development, and economic stabilization efforts as evidence of their success. They also launched an initiative to improve institutional openness and accountability. These developments are encouraging. They are occurring, however, in a context of no progress on issues that are of profound concern to the Afghan people and the international community. The severe restrictions on women and girls, exclusionary governance, a human rights crisis, and the continued presence of terrorist groups that threaten Afghanistan, the region, and international peace and security. In line with my last briefing to this Council, we assess that the de facto authorities face no significant armed or political threat. However, key risks to the country's stability are accumulating and mainly stem from the de facto authorities' own policies. Recent events in Badakhshan Province illustrate these risks. While the armed clashes, as detailed in the Secretary-General's report, did not threaten de facto authority control, they show what can happen when local communities are excluded from decision-making, resource sharing, and economic opportunity. During my recent visit to Badakhshan, people told me they seek opportunities, basic services, education, and a future for their children, not exclusion. Over the past three months, events in Herat province remained similarly concerning. UNAMA documented arrests of women and girls related to strict enforcement of the de facto authorities' dress code. Subsequent protests were met with the excessive use of force. The de facto authorities continue to carry out arrests of women, including over the past week, for alleged violation of the dress code. Across the country, UNAMA also documented mounting pressure on minority communities, media outlet closures, and arrests and intimidation of journalists. These incidents are part of the broader trend of coercive social regulation that is alienating many communities. UNAMA is engaging with the de facto authorities on these critical concerns in Kabul and through our field offices. Mr. President, this month, UNAMA released a report on the experiences of victims of Afghanistan's decades-long conflict. 95% of people we interviewed in Afghanistan reported continued psychological and emotional harm. including depression, anxiety, trauma, and flashbacks. Many are still living with disability, chronic pain, and loss of livelihoods. The findings remind us that peace is not only the absence of armed conflict. Sustainable peace requires dignity, inclusion, opportunity, and hope. Many Afghans tell us that the last five years of relative stability have provided a welcome breathing space. Yet they also tell us they are suffering under the rigid social policies of the de facto authorities and from Afghanistan's fragile economic and humanitarian situation. While Afghanistan has maintained a degree of macroeconomic stability, this does not equate to recovery. Economic growth has not kept pace with the rising population or made-up for declining aid. Per capita income has dropped by 5.6% and exports are down. Afghanistan remains heavily dependent on imports with border disruptions and wider regional instability contributing to weakened household purchasing power. Food insecurity and malnutrition present a serious concern. UNICEF reports that some 3.7 million children are suffering from deficient malnutrition, including some 1 million children experiencing severe acute malnutrition. The 2026 humanitarian needs response plan is only 30% funded. Humanitarian organizations are being forced to make hard choices on where they operate, whom they can reach, and which services they can maintain. Health facilities, nutrition centers, women's protection services, and other essential programs have closed or scaled back due to funding cuts. At the same time, Afghanistan continues to experience an extreme demographic and socioeconomic shock. This year alone, nearly 1.2 million Afghans have returned from Pakistan and Iran, with total returns reaching 6.5 million since 2023. Without sustained support, for returnees and host communities, competition over scarce resources, risks fueling grievances, increasing displacement, and promoting instability. The de facto authorities ban on opium poppy cultivation has been a positive measure with huge decreases in cultivation, but risks bouncing back because of the economic pressures. Greater support for alternative livelihoods is crucial, as is sustained and principled humanitarian and development assistance for the Afghan people. Mr. President, no discussion of Afghanistan can ignore the continued exclusion of women and girls. The words of an Afghan woman we met in Kandahar represents their experience, and I quote: If we follow one rule, another one comes next. Women wearing hijab were instructed to wear a mask. Those wearing masks are told to wear a burqa. Those wearing a burqa are questioned about the absence of a mahram, and those accompanied by a mahram are questioned about the relationship with him. By denying access By denying women access to education, professions, and public life, the de facto authorities are not safeguarding Afghanistan's future. They are constraining the talent and productivity needed for post-conflict recovery. This is at odds with their stated vision of a prosperous, self-reliant, and sovereign Afghanistan that can attract international investment. This fund marks one year since restrictions preventing Afghan women from accessing UN premises, including national female UN personnel, were enforced. This is a violation of UN principles and a serious operational constraint. Humanitarian actors report difficulty reaching women and girls. Male-only delivery models cannot replace the participation of Afghan women staff and organizations cannot consult women, assess risks, or verify that assistance reaches those who need it most. Funding cuts are compounding the problem. Nearly three-quarters of Afghan women-led organizations have seen reduced funding over the past year. while more than 80% report increasing needs among women and girls. At a moment when Afghan women face unprecedented restrictions, international support mechanisms for them are decreasing. Across Afghanistan, Afghan women tell us that engagement, assistance, and support from the international community represent what they call points of hope. We urge international partners to prioritize support for Afghan women and girls. Above all, we again call on the de facto authorities to end all restrictions on women and girls. Mr. President, relations between Afghanistan and Pakistan remain another matter of serious concern. The effects of sporadic hostilities and the almost year-long border closure are taking an increasing toll on civilians, communities, and businesses. UNAMA continues to encourage de-escalation and dialogue to resolve differences, including on the presence of terrorist groups in Afghanistan, as reported by the Sanctions Monitoring Team. We welcome ongoing regional mediation efforts. Mr. President, as the High Commissioner for Refugees and the UNDP Administrator cautioned during a joint visit to Afghanistan in July, Developments in Afghanistan do not necessarily stay in Afghanistan. Instability, increased out-migration and displacement, radicalization, and growing insecurity have regional and international consequences. Sustained international engagement, including through the Doha Process, remains essential. Currently, the Doha Process is the multilateral framework through which such engagement is occurring, aimed at Afghanistan's reintegration into the international community based on compliance with international obligations and commitments. This structured engagement among the de facto authorities, the international community, and a wide range of Afghan stakeholders has identified key issues and positions expanded dialogue, and in some areas, built confidence. The main obstacle to progress is the de facto authorities' preference for bilateral approaches over multilateral engagement, which they view as undermining their claims of sovereignty. They continue, however, to participate in working groups on counter-narcotics in the private sector and engage on some key political issues. What is now needed is a clear indication from the de facto authorities of their willingness to address the wider concerns of the international community. To this end, the de facto authorities can take steps toward inclusive governance and the lifting of restrictions on women and girls, and show they are meeting their counterterrorism commitments. Member states can reinforce that Afghanistan's reintegration into the international system is possible through concrete, balanced, cooperative steps that begin to address the key issues preventing reintegration. Mr. President, we remain confident in the value of principled and pragmatic engagement. It sustains dialogue on the key issues and concerns, maintains influence, reduces risks, creates opportunities for progress, and critically, supports the needs and aspirations of the Afghan people. Thank you.
I thank Ms. Gagnon for her briefing. Rest assured, the Council supports UNAMIR's work and your own work. I now give the floor to Ms. Najis Niran.

Thank you very much, Mr. President, members of the Council. Thank you for having me here today. One month ago, 15 August, marked the five years since the Taliban seized control of our country. On August 15, 2021, we did not witness only the collapse of the Islamic Republic of Afghanistan. We also witnessed the erosion of universal values, international commitments, and most profoundly, the norms and standards for the protection of human rights and dignity of women. While the situation keeps deteriorating, Afghanistan is being allowed to slip from the international view. The voice of Afghan women have been heard, but not acted upon. The recommendations of the UN independent assessment have gone largely ignored. The call for inclusive governance have fallen on deaf ears. And the distance between what is discussed in this chamber and the reality faced by Afghans on the ground keeps growing. Mr. President, a few days ago, I spoke to my sisters in Afghanistan. and asked them what message they would like me to deliver today. Let me share three quotes that remained with me. First, when I listen to statements of the international community about Afghan women, I feel as if I'm burning in pain and someone is reading a novel to help me forget my pain for a few minutes. Two, being a woman is a crime. And being born as a woman in Afghanistan is an even greater crime. Three, is five years not enough to convince the world that the Taliban have not and will not change? Mr. President, I'm sure you can feel the pain behind these words, the pain of being denied education and work, the pain of seeing your dreams crushed, and above all, the pain of being told you're nothing time and again. In five years, the Taliban have issued scores of decrees, stripping women and girls of all our basic human rights and fundamental freedoms. Today, women are allowed to beg for a loaf of bread, but they are not allowed to work and have a dignified income. A father is not allowed to send his daughter to school, but can marry her off as young as eight years old to a man as old as 70 years old. or just sell her for $500. According to UNICEF, Afghanistan is projected to lose 25,000 female health workers by 2013, with no human resource to fill this gap. And according to UNFPA, we are again losing more than 600 mothers per 100,000 live births, mostly due to preventable and treatable disease and conditions. Today, what's happening to women and girls in Afghanistan is a political femicide and the worst form of gender apartheid. Mr. President, the crisis in Afghanistan also affect boys. Although they continue to have access to education, the content and character of education have changed significantly. Today, the number of madrassas has surpassed the number of schools in Afghanistan. Several reports produced by credible national and international organizations highlight widespread concern about changes in the attitude and behavior of boys attending madrassas. Afghanistan under Taliban rule is once again becoming a safe haven for international terrorist groups and a hub for religious madrassas, producing tens and thousands of young men at risk of radicalization. Mr. President, The rise of religious extremism in Afghanistan must concern all of us. Unfortunately, we all know too well the consequence of radicalism. The lessons of the past should not need to be repeated because we have seen what happens in Afghanistan does not stay in Afghanistan. Mr. President, Afghanistan's crisis is a profound human rights and humanitarian catastrophe. but its roots are above all political. What we need for Afghanistan is a political solution. Addressing women's rights cannot be separated from inclusive government and inclusive governance. We need a credible and inclusive Afghan-led political process in which women and men across ethnic and religious lines can chart a shared vision for our country. Today, Afghan political actors, civil society, and women are building a genuine unity of purpose with very little international support. The Taliban have shown no interest in a political process. But their refusal cannot become an excuse to push Afghanistan further down the international agenda. The Afghan opposition is doing its part. Bringing the Taliban to the table is a task for others. including the members of this Council. Mr. President, five years Afghan women have not been passive victims. We have organized, advocated, documented violations, delivered aid, supported survivors, and engaged governments, parliaments, the United Nations, and this chamber. At the moment, we are developing our roadmap to justice and reconciliation. focusing on accountability, intra-Afghan dialogue, and a political pathway for Afghanistan, as we do not see the rights of women isolated from other issues and crises in Afghanistan. Mr. President, we are doing all this under enormous pressure, with shrinking civic space, increasing risk, and declining resources. The past five years have been highly challenging for Afghan women, but we know the journey to justice is not easy. and we remain committed even if it gets more challenging. Mr. President, according to OCHA, Afghanistan humanitarian response plan for 2026 requires approximately 1.7 billion. Yet only a small fraction of that requirement has been funded. This raises a fundamental question about the international community's response. Can we honestly say that our response has gone beyond statements and expression of concern? Mr. President, solidarity must produce action. Afghan women cannot afford another year of waiting for the world to decide what to do with Afghanistan, how to deal with the Taliban, and whether or not to support Afghan women. Mr. President, we need clarity, political will, and a pathway from commitment to action, and we need it now. I therefore put forward three concrete proposals for the Council. One, pass a resolution recognizing the institutionalized discrimination against women and girls in Afghanistan and declaring the Council's commitment to support us in our pursuit of justice and accountability. The resolution should also ask Australia, Canada, Germany, and Netherlands to speed up the case of Afghanistan to ICJ. Ask the International Criminal Court to issue more arrest warrants against the leadership of the Taliban. And ask the member states to recognize the situation in Afghanistan as gender apartheid and codify it as a crime against humanity. Two, support an inclusive Afghan political pathway for Afghanistan. The enormous strategic review offers an opportunity to advance the recommendations of the independent assessment and require the Doha process to become inclusive by engaging not only Taliban, but also all other political and civil society groups from inside Afghanistan and as well as from exile, with the end state of inclusive government and inclusive governance for Afghanistan. Three, we call on the international community to scale up humanitarian support to Afghanistan and fully fund the 1.7 billion response plan as an urgent priority. The support should be targeted those most left behind. Mr. President, The world knows what is happening in Afghanistan. The question is whether the international community is prepared to act on what it knows or not. Thank you.
I thank Ms. Nahon for her briefing. I now give the floor to Council members wishing to make a statement. I now give the floor to the representative of China.

President, I thank Deputy Special Representative Gan Yun and Ms. Nehan for their briefings. Over the past five years, with the active efforts of the Afghan government, the situation in Afghanistan has remained generally stable, with positive progress in areas such as economic reconstruction, combating narcotics, and external engagement, among others. At the same time, Afghanistan is still faced with complex challenges in the humanitarian, development, women's rights, and counterterrorism fields, among others. The international community should view the situation in Afghanistan in a comprehensive and objective manner. and take integrated measures, and play a constructive role in helping Afghanistan realize lasting peace and stability at an early date. I wish to stress a few points. First, engagement and dialogue should continue to be strengthened. All parties should cherish the outcomes of engagement and dialogue with the Afghan government, show good faith, and stay patient. And on the basis of respecting Afghanistan's national conditions and stage of development, enhance pragmatic communication with Afghanistan on issues of mutual concerns to constantly enhance mutual trust and address differences, and help Afghanistan to gradually integrate into the international community. China supports regional platforms such as the foreign ministers' meeting among the neighboring countries of Afghanistan and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization together with the Doha Process in forming greater synergies in stabilizing and helping Afghanistan. The Security Council should resume as soon as possible the package arrangements for travel ban exemptions of the 1988 Sanctions Mechanism to provide necessary facilitation for international engagement. We welcome the appointment of USG Fatima as SRSG for Afghanistan. and support UNAMA in playing a better role as a bridge for communication and in fully and effectively implementing all its mandates. Second, we must support Afghanistan in improving livelihoods. At present, nearly half of the Afghan population needs humanitarian assistance. One third of the people are facing acute food insecurity. and 3.7 million children under the age of five and 1.2 million pregnant and breastfeeding women are acutely malnourished. Yet only 30% of this year's humanitarian funding for the country is in place. Due to sharp declines in external aid, large numbers of assistance programs were forced to close, which, combined with other factors such as returning refugees and natural disasters, will likely make the humanitarian crisis in Afghanistan even worse. We call on all parties, in particular traditional donors, to take urgent action to promptly fill the funding gap and avoid politicizing humanitarian issues. It must be stressed that development is the fundamental path for Afghanistan to overcome the humanitarian crisis and its dependence on foreign aid. We commend the efforts of UNOPS, UNDP, UNHCR and other UN agencies. and expect the two working groups on private sector and counter-narcotics of the Doha process to achieve more practical outcomes. Relevant countries should effectively bear its historical responsibilities by immediately resuming aid to Afghanistan, lifting unilateral sanctions on the country promptly, returning the overseas assets of the Afghan Central Bank and providing necessary resources for Afghanistan's reconstruction and development. Third, the fundamental rights and interests of the people must be safeguarded. Reports by the UN have pointed out repeatedly that the restrictive policies facing Afghan women and girls in education, employment, healthcare, and public life not only affect the physical and mental health of women, but also undermine social stability and development prospects, hindering Afghanistan from gaining greater international support. According to UNICEF, restrictions on women's education and employment cost Afghanistan's economy at least $84 million annually. We call upon the Afghan government to prioritize the long-term development of the country and the fundamental interests of the people effectively guarantee the fundamental rights and interests of all Afghans, including Afghan women, so that they will have an opportunity to contribute to developing and building the country. The Afghan female UN staff have played an indispensable role in humanitarian assistance and other efforts, We call upon the Afghan Government to lift the restrictions on fulfilling their mandate without delay and provide due facilitation for the work of UN agencies. Fourth, terrorism must be resolutely eradicated. Terrorism is the common enemy of humanity. ISIL, al-Qaeda, ETIM, and TTP, among others, are terrorist organizations listed by the Security Council. All countries have the obligation to firmly combat them, and there should be no room for ambiguity. We take note of Afghanistan's efforts to combat ISIL-K, and urge Afghanistan to demonstrate greater resolve and efforts to eradicate all terrorist forces within its borders at an early date, and to respond in a concrete manner to the common concerns of the international community. We also expect Afghanistan to engage actively in dialogue and cooperation in counterterrorism with countries in the region to constantly enhance strategic mutual trust and jointly safeguard regional security. As a friendly neighbor of Afghanistan, China stands ready to continue working with the international community in the tireless efforts in support of Afghanistan's peace, stability, development, and prosperity. I thank you, President.
I thank the representative of China for their statement and I give the floor to the representative of the Russian Federation.

President, we would like to thank today's briefers. We wish to welcome the appointment of Rabab Fatimi as head of UNAMA. We expect that the new head of mission will consistently assist the strengthening of trust between the Afghan authorities and the international community, as well as facilitate the provision of comprehensive assistance to the country. Therein lies the key to genuine, pragmatic engagement with Afghanistan. There is no alternative to this path, nor will there be. Russia has consistently supported UNAMIR's efforts within the limits of UNAMIR's mandate. However, we believe that all functions should be fulfilled evenly and in full. We've taken note of the SG's report about the situation in the country. We'd like to state the following. Five years ago, The two-decades-long occupation of Afghanistan came to an end following an irresponsible withdrawal of foreign forces from the country. The Taliban movement acceded to power. And every time we've met in this Chamber to discuss the situation in the country, we've heard those representing countries whose military contingents hastily left the country, we heard them saying that Afghanistan is on the cusp of collapse, it's on the cusp of becoming a black hole. Yet these gloomy forecasts, thankfully, did not come to pass. This was achieved in no small part thanks to the Taliban betting on multifaceted development of regional cooperation focused on building an independent and self-reliant state. Despite ongoing stifling sanctions, the government is working meticulously to fix the current state of affairs. Kabul stands ready to engage in constructive cooperation with any country on the basis of mutual respect and a search for common ground. Yet it's plain that the Afghans will have trouble setting off down the path of sustainable development and prosperity acting alone. Afghanistan still needs our common, unpoliticized support. President, Russia has unswervingly believed that it's important to ensure a realistic, comprehensive approach to Afghanistan. This is based on an objective analysis, a balanced assessment of the situation in Afghanistan, genuine constructive engagement by the international community on the Afghan file, fully factoring in the needs of the Afghans themselves. trust-based dialogue with the authorities covering all issues. Now, this dialogue must be fully free from the language of pressure and blackmail. Such a comprehensive approach has the support of all regional players without exception. First and foremost, the participants in the Moscow format and its regional quad, as well as the CSTO, the SCO, including the CSTO working group on Afghanistan and the SCO Afghanistan contact group. We welcome the fact that Pragmatic cooperation with the Taliban is also part and parcel of the so-called mosaic approach put forward by UNAMA, including as regards diplomatic representation, the lifting of sanctions and freezing assets, as well as the fight against the terrorist threat and the narcotic drugs threat. Timely resolving these problems without any preconditions being imposed is the direct path to international reintegration of Afghanistan. Selective and biased approaches, as well as the fixation on human rights something that's only of interest to a group of Western donors, all of these are a dead end. We regret that not all Western donors have learned the lessons of their past mistakes. They are doggedly imposing their line on UNAMA, a line based on threats and ultimatums. given the doubts some Security Council members harbor about the future of the mission. This is a dangerous game they're playing. It could threaten the entire UN presence in the country. Plus, the Taliban itself is unlikely to be interested in the UN keeping an eye on it, so to speak, solely to serve the interests of those who intervened and then were cast out of Afghanistan in 2021. President, we are disquieted by ongoing tensions between Afghanistan and Pakistan. against the backdrop of terrorist activities by TTP. We call on friendly countries to return to the search for a solution to this problem only on a political and diplomatic track. On our side, we are always ready to provide support and assistance to our friends. We hope that mutually beneficial cooperation between the parties will resume, including on the fight against terrorism. We are still concerned by the fact terrorist groups are still present in Afghanistan, ISIL-Khorasan and the East Turkestan Islamic Movement, ETIM. Despite the authorities' efforts, it has not been possible to buck the trend completely. These groups continue to maintain their capacity, accruing resources by recruiting new members and also by securing illegal financial flows for its activities. ISIL Fighters are continuing to harbor hopes of building their own caliphate, using any opportunity to destabilize the situation in the country and in the region as a whole. We are paying particular attention to foreign terrorist fighters who have accumulated experience in Syria and Iraq. Regrettably, to this day, it's very difficult to assess the scale of these fighters' use of weapons left behind by NATO. the drug threat is inextricably linked to terrorism. We cannot but commend the Taliban's work on combating the cultivation of the opium poppy. Having said that, we should pay heightened attention to countering the production and trade of and in synthetic drugs so as to buck the incipient negative trend. In order to ensure full eradication of the drug threat, we need broad-based regional and international cooperation, including under the auspices of relevant bodies such as UNODC. We attach particular attention to the socioeconomic situation country. We welcome the selfless efforts of humanitarian agencies and humanitarian personnel. They're working under difficult conditions, including conditions resulting from the consequences of the military aggression of the U.S. and Israel against the Islamic Republic of Iran. They're also facing chronic underfinancing. Despite this, they continue to provide help to those in need. We are disquieted by the food supply problems in Afghanistan. We are of the view that, under the circumstances, UNAMA should focus on its mandate, that is, amplifying steps to unfreeze assets and to assist development. We believe that Western donors trumpeting about the situation of women and girls in the country We hope that they will join efforts to support the country in creating dignified conditions for women and girls to live in a stable, prosperous state. Russia is constantly supporting the people of Afghanistan. We stand ready to broaden our partnership with Afghanistan across all areas, including on regional security. We're interested in strengthening trade and economic the trade and economic potential of Afghanistan, as well as dialogue with representatives of local business, including as part of relevant industry fora organized by Russia. We are following very closely the situation as regards human rights and fundamental freedoms in Afghanistan, including the inalienable right to education and work for all people in Afghanistan, including women and girls, and this irrespective of their ethnicity, religion, and their sex. This is an imperative. We're tracking work on establishing a genuinely inclusive government with the participation of all ethnic and political groups in the country. We are counting on progress being made on both of the aforementioned fronts. President, the Russian Federation genuinely supports the aspirations of the Afghan people to live in a peaceful, prosperous country free from terrorism and narcotic drugs. Regional stability as a whole hinges on the situation in Afghanistan. We reiterate our calls for the UN to ensure we engage with those Afghans who directly represent the real authorities and genuinely bear responsibility for what is happening in the country. That's the only way to solve the country's problems and to genuinely reintegrate Afghanistan into the international community.

I thank you.
I thank the representative of the Russian Federation for his statement, and I give the floor now to the representative of Pakistan.

Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to thank the officer in charge and deputy SRSG, UNAMA, Georgie Ghanem, for her briefing, and we take note of the report of the Secretary-General. Let me also welcome the appointment of SRSG and head of UNAMA, for this important position, and we look forward to working closely with her. Let me also thank Nargis Nehan for her remarks. She rightly mentioned the world knows what's happening in Afghanistan. I must say that Madam presents a good example of how Afghan refugees including women in particular, who are in Pakistan, rose to prominent positions in many fields in their lives. President, over half a decade since the Taliban takeover, Pakistan, as the immediate neighbor, has made rigorous efforts to help ameliorate the suffering of our Afghan brothers and sisters. Pakistan engaged at high levels, facilitated humanitarian relief efforts, provided visa exceptions for vulnerable Afghans, and trade and transit incentives to boost the economy, and participated in various regional cooperation initiatives, including connectivity projects. and remained at the forefront of efforts to stabilize Afghanistan and facilitate its integration with the international community. And despite reservations with regard to certain policies of the Taliban, Pakistan abided by its international commitments to allow unhindered humanitarian aid to Afghanistan. As noted in the SD's report, at least 687 humanitarian cargo trucks entered Afghanistan from Pakistan during the reporting period. Unfortunately, the hopes and expectations of the international community at that critical juncture five years ago did not materialize and, in fact, gradually turned into despair and disappointment. The extent of challenges in Afghanistan is evident, including from the briefing by the Deputy SRSG. And the SD's report highlights that the semblance of relative stability that the Taliban seek to display masks the accumulating risks that could impact the country's stability over the short and long term. And we agree with the assessment that the risks associated with human rights violations, lack of political inclusivity, acute economic pressure, and the increasing terrorist threat from Afghanistan are a cause of grave concern for the international community. Most indicators in Afghanistan present a declining trend. Afghanistan has once again become a safe haven for numerous terrorist groups operating with impunity from its soil. The humanitarian needs and response plan remains severely underfunded. A highly centralized system of governance is in place, devoid of political inclusivity. Human rights violations, including arbitrary killings and tightening of restrictions against women and girls, have intensified. And as we have heard, the economy remains on life support, largely from donors. President, terrorism has been at the core of Afghanistan's problems. This finds its roots in the deep nexus between the Taliban and terrorist groups, such as the TTP, the BLS, and its Mujib Brigade, ISIL-K, ETIM, and their affiliates that are operating with impunity on Afghan soil And the situation made worse by external actors, the spoilers who support proxies inside Afghanistan to target Pakistan and other neighboring countries. That is the unfortunate reality on ground. And it is Pakistan that is most directly impacted, paying a heavy cost. Over the last three years alone, more than 4,700 innocent Pakistanis have lost their lives to terrorism emanating from Afghanistan. So no country would tolerate such a situation. We expected that the Taliban would take concrete and verifiable actions against those terrorist groups. Regrettably, they failed to act. in complete disregard for the legitimate security concerns of Pakistan and other countries. We hope that the Taliban will follow through on their word, honor their commitments made to the international community. The presence of advanced weapons and equipment, including drones, and huge cache of multibillion dollar worth of arms and ammunition left behind by international forces which was meant for use by the previous Afghan government, continues to pose a serious threat. We had hoped to see some analysis on INAMMA's efforts to prevent and address the illicit trade in and destabilizing accumulation of small arms and light weapons and their diversion in Afghanistan and the region, which is part of INAMMA's mandate. NAMA should also report on the illicit Afghan economy that facilitates terror financing and money laundering through hundi and hawala networks. President, Taliban's refusal to publicly denounce and condemn terrorist groups is evidence enough of their complicity and active support for these groups. Pakistan cannot sit idle in the face of this terrorist onslaught. We will respond in self-defense as and when needed and in accordance with international law. We will defend ourselves against whosoever attempts to harm our citizens and our national security. President, the humanitarian, the deteriorating humanitarian human rights situation also demonstrates the Taliban's continued backtracking on their international obligations. Women and girls are denied their fundamental freedoms and basic dignity with discriminatory and abusive practices that contravene Islamic laws, traditions, and tenets of Muslim faith. From 12th to 13th July earlier this year, Pakistan hosted the 9th Ministerial Conference on Women in Islamabad, where the OIC adopted Islamabad Declaration, which expressed concern over Taliban's continued restrictions on women and girls as being inconsistent with Islamic values. For over four decades, Pakistan welcomed millions of Afghan refugees, despite insufficient international support. and also dealt with huge caseloads of illegal Afghans, including those without documentation, who pose a serious threat to our security. We continue to facilitate vulnerable Afghans numbering thousands, despite limitations. While we provide all possible facilitation, the international community must step up and shoulder its responsibility. President, we look forward to the next steps of the UN-led Doha process and action plan, the mosaic approach to address Afghanistan's multifaceted challenges comprehensively, with well-defined objectives and a realistic roadmap as the only viable pathway for normalization. Pakistan and Afghanistan our immediate neighbors, having historical relations and fraternal bonds with civilizational links. And peace and stability in Afghanistan is in Pakistan's national interest. Lasting peace and prosperity would require the Taliban to demonstrate responsible behavior, to fulfill its international obligations, to be seen as a reliable partner in the region, and for the wider international community. Pakistan, on its part, remains committed to working with all partners for durable peace and stability in Afghanistan and the welfare of its people. I thank you.
I thank the representative of Pakistan for his statements, and I give the floor to the representative of the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, it's my honor to deliver this statement on behalf of the A3, namely Liberia, Somalia, and my own country, the Democratic Republic of the Congo. We thank Ms. Georgette Kanyondo, as well as Ms. Nihan, for their exhaustive briefings. The A3 congratulates Dr. Rabab Fatima on her appointment as the head of the United Nations Assistance Mission in Afghanistan. We are confident that she will successfully carry out the responsibilities entrusted to her. The A3 takes note of her commitment to engage in broad consultations with Afghan, regional, and international stakeholders as well as her determination to place the promotion and protection of the rights of women and girls at the heart of her mandate. At the outset, the A3 remain concerned by the complex political, humanitarian and socio-economic challenges facing Afghanistan. The Afghan people continue to endure the consequences of economic hardship, acute poverty and limited access to essential services. The A/3 reaffirms the importance of sustained international engagement in support of the Afghan people. In this regard, we would like to highlight the following points. First, the A/3 reiterates its strong support for the continued work of UNAMA. We underline the critical role played by UNAMA as a key platform for international engagement, political dialogue, human rights monitoring, and the coordination of humanitarian and development efforts in Afghanistan. With this in mind, we emphasize the importance of ensuring that the mission is able to operate in conditions that allow it to effectively carry out its mandate, including through safe and unhindered access for United Nations personnel and partners, free from interference. Second, the A3 expresses deep concern over the worsening humanitarian situation in Afghanistan, as the cumulative effects of declining international assistance, large-scale returns of displaced populations, and natural disasters, including recent flash floods, continue to exert immense pressure on Afghan communities. We are gravely alarmed by the sharp deterioration in food security, with 13.8 million people projected to face acute food insecurity and nearly 4.9 million children and mothers suffering from acute malnutrition. The arrival of nearly 1.15 million returnees so far in 2026, places severe pressure on local absorption capacities, while the 2026 humanitarian needs and response plan remains critically underfunded at only 29.9%. The A3 commends the persistent efforts of the UN and international partners who are working under extremely challenging conditions and urges donors to act swiftly in order to close the funding gaps. The humanitarian challenges facing Afghanistan are not isolated. They reflect broader realities affecting millions of people across the world. The A3 therefore reiterates that civilian protection, humanitarian access, and international solidarity must remain universal principles applied consistently and without distinction. Third, the A3 recognizes that the full participation of women and girls is the cornerstone for Afghanistan's successful reintegration into the international community. We emphasize that ensuring access to education, employment, fundamental freedoms, and meaningful participation in society will unlock the nation's full potential and uphold the dignity of its people. We are also concerned by ongoing restrictions preventing United Nations Afghan women personnel from accessing United Nations premises and carrying out life-saving operations. In that regard, we echo the calls of the international community and call on the authorities to permit United Nations national female personnel and national female personnel to return to their places of work. Fourth, the A3 remains concerned by the continued threats posed by terrorist groups operating within Afghanistan and reaffirms that its territory should not be used as a platform for terrorist activities that jeopardize the security and safety of neighboring states and pose threats to international peace and security. Furthermore, we urge countries of the region to intensify support for efforts to address and counter threats from terrorist organizations operating in Afghan territory. In this regard, we underline the importance of the Security Council sanctions regime concerning Afghanistan and reiterate our support for the work of the 1988 Sanctions Committee. Fifth, the A/3 reiterates that Engagement between the international community and Afghanistan is crucial for Afghanistan's sustainable peace, stability, and social and economic development. We welcome the structured engagement through the Doha process, including the working groups on the private sector and counter-narcotics, and note the Secretary-General's call on all members of the Doha process and on the Afghan authorities to further engage in the proposed comprehensive approach as envisaged by Security Council resolution 2721 towards the objective of achieving an Afghanistan that is fully reintegrated into the international community. To conclude, Mr. President, the A3 reiterates its strong commitment to the sovereignty, independence, territorial integrity and national unity of Afghanistan. We stress the importance of a coordinated and integrated approach among political, humanitarian and development actors in order to better address the multiple challenges facing the Afghan people. We reaffirm our steadfast solidarity with the people of Afghanistan and our commitment to help them in their pursuit of lasting peace, security, stability and sustainable development. Thank you.
I thank the representative of the Democratic Republic of the Congo for your statement on behalf of the A3. And I now give the floor to the representative of Latvia.

Thank you, President.

And I also let me thank the deputies, our SG, for Afghanistan, Ms. Rosita Ganyo, for her comprehensive briefing. As a woman from Nangarhar told UN Women, "Even if I have hopes or dreams, I know I will not be able to achieve them because it is not what is expected of women." End of quote. I thank the representative of Latvia for their statement. I now give the floor to the representative of the United States.

Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you to the briefers. Nor will we be intimidated or coerced by a Taliban regime that cruelly uses American citizens as bargaining chips or some kind of leverage in its ill-fated pursuit of international legitimacy. In March, in fact, Secretary of State Rubio designated Afghanistan under the Taliban regime as a state sponsor of wrongful detention as it kidnaps citizens of not just Americans, but of dozens of nationalities every day for ransom and political concessions. That restriction has now been in place for a full year. The Secretary General has stated, and of course we agree, that it is a violation of international law, including the UN Charter, and it's obstructing lifesaving assistance to Afghanistan. And it's a critical impediment, obviously, to Afghanistan's reintegration into the international community colleagues, let's just think about that contradiction. The Taliban wants a seat at the international table. They want a seat here. Yet they're barring women from walking through the front door of the United Nations in their own country. Again, yet they want a seat here. So this council has spoken. Resolution 2822 said the erosion of the rights of women and girls and minorities is so severe that their absence makes peace, stability, and prosperity unattainable. That same resolution extended UNAMA through June of 2027, streamlining and focusing its work. The United States welcomes that reform and expects UNAMA to demonstrate measurable value, particularly as it remains the most expensive political mission. We also welcome the Secretary General's appointment in July of Rabab Fatima. I've had the pleasure of meeting with her and wish her luck and health as she takes on this difficult task as a special representative. We look forward to her early engagement with this council, with colleagues. There is a larger question here. How many UN reports documenting abuse How many council resolutions demanding change, how many years of engagement can we pass before we see measurable results? We will be watching closely for evidence that the revised mandate and new leadership are translating into a leaner, more accountable mission and focusing on the work that matters most. The same applies for the UN-led Doha process. The comprehensive approach can provide a path forward, but only if the Taliban engages seriously and meets its commitments. Colleagues, this council must demand results from the Taliban regime. We need to see actions, not words, and that will determine whether Afghanistan moves forward towards peace and legitimacy and the Afghan people. Many soldiers from many of our countries for many years and civilians as well fought so valiantly so that they could have a better future. And I certainly agree with the notion of what happens in Afghanistan does not stay in Afghanistan. Thank you, colleagues.
I thank the representative of the United States for their statement. I now give the floor to the representative of Denmark.

Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President. Let me also thank Deputy SIDS Gagnon and Mrs. Nehan for their important briefings. We meet at a critical moment for Afghanistan. Last month marked five years since the Taliban seized power, and just days ago we marked 25 years since the terrorist attacks of September 11. But both occasions carry important lessons for this Council. They remind us why Afghanistan remains a matter of which this Council is seized, and why sustained international attention remains essential. I will focus on three points. First, across Afghanistan, human rights and fundamental freedoms remain severely restricted. Civic space continues to shrink, while journalists, civil society and human rights defenders face growing pressure. For women and girls, the situation is particularly grave. The Taliban pursues a deliberate policy of gender-based segregation, thus systematically excluding women and girls from public life and imposing sweeping restrictions on virtually every aspect of their lives, from education and employment to freedom of movement and participation in society. These restrictions are reinforced by an increasingly repressive and institutional framework, which further deny women and girls access to justice, protection, and essential services. The dire consequences of the Taliban's systematic discrimination and repression are not only devastating for the lives, the dignity, and opportunities of Afghan women and girls. They also undermine Afghanistan's social and economic development, stability, and prospects for lasting peace and international reintegration. The international community has been clear in its response. In a joint statement delivered by Denmark last month on behalf of 57 countries, we called for an end to the systematic discrimination of women and girls, and for the rights and dignity of all Afghans to be upheld. And we reiterate these calls firmly today. Second, Mr. President, the ability of the United Nations and humanitarian actors to operate effectively and without undue hindrances must always be safeguarded. As we have heard, September marks one year since Afghan female UN personnel were prevented from accessing UN premises across the country. This is completely unacceptable. It is contrary to international law. And it directly undermines the ability of the UN to fulfill its mandate. This is particularly concerning amid a continuous and severe humanitarian crisis, fueled by exclusion, by discrimination, and by a basic lack of respect for human rights. Nearly 22 million Afghans require humanitarian assistance. Meanwhile, large-scale returns from neighboring countries are placing further pressure on already vulnerable communities, where needs by far outstrip available resources. The full participation of Afghan women is critical to an effective and principled humanitarian response. We call on the Taliban to urgently reverse all restrictions on UN and humanitarian personnel, and to allow them to carry out their work safely and without discrimination or interference. Mr. President, thirdly, Afghanistan continues to face significant security threats, including from terrorist groups operating from within its territory. The continued presence and activity of terrorist groups such as TTP, Al-Qaeda, and ISIL-K remain a serious concern for Afghanistan, its neighbors, and international peace and security. As we recently commemorated the victims of September 11, we recall that Afghanistan must never again become a safe haven for terrorism. We call on the Taliban to take concrete, sustained, and verifiable action against all terrorist groups operating in or from Afghanistan. In closing, Mr. President, international engagement must remain principled and focused on tangible outcomes for the Afghan people. The Doha process has an important role to play. But progress towards greater international integration must go hand in hand with significant improvements on human rights, on inclusive governments, counter-terrorism, and Afghanistan's international obligations. UNAMA remains an indispensable part of this effort. And Denmark warmly welcomes the newly appointed SSG, Mrs. Rabab Fatima. We look forward to working closely with her as she takes forward this important mandate. Thank you.

Mr. President, Colombia aligns itself with the request for language that allows us to move forward as a Security Council on a possible condemnation of the Taliban state, not only due to the institutional and non-institutional exclusion of women and millions of girls, which is a generational problem. I thank the representative of Colombia for their statement. I now give the floor to the representative of Bahrain.

Thank you, Mr. President. At the outset, I'd like to thank Madam Georgette Gagnon. the deputy SRSG in Afghanistan, and Ms. Narjis Nihan, the representative of civil society, for their briefings. Mr. President, in light of the continued challenges that are facing Afghanistan over five years since the de facto authorities took over control of the country, the Kingdom of Bahrain reaffirms the importance of moving from managing the status quo to making available the necessary conditions to make steady and gradual progress towards reintegrating Afghanistan in the international community. This requires making tangible progress by the authorities in Afghanistan and responding to the legitimate concerns of the international community and fulfilling Afghanistan's international commitments. We also reaffirmed the importance of allowing women and girls to exercise their right to education, employment, and participation in public life, considering their participation important and vital for the future of Afghanistan, its development, and its stability. And the activities of terrorist parties in Afghanistan is a source of extreme concern, and we stressed the need for Afghan territory not to be allowed to become safe havens or a source to threaten any other country, with the importance of enhancing regional and international cooperation in this track.
