I thank the representative of the Kingdom of Bahrain for that statement and hand the floor to the representative of the United Kingdom.

Thank you, President. I thank Deputy Special Representative Gagnon and Najeh Snehan for their briefings. Let me begin by expressing our deep appreciation to UNAMA for its vital work. We welcome the appointment of Special Representative Reba Fatima and reaffirm our strong commitment to UNAMA's success. Today, I want to highlight three points. First, the UK strongly condemns the Taliban's systematic discrimination against women and girls. No country can prosper while half its population is excluded from public life. The Taliban must respect the fundamental rights and freedoms of all Afghans in accordance with international law. Last week marked one year since the Taliban barred Afghan women working for the United Nations from accessing UN premises. We pay tribute to UN staff across Afghanistan for their dedication and professionalism, and I pay testament to the extraordinary resilience of the women of Afghanistan. We call on the Taliban to lift this unacceptable restriction, which continues to hamper the delivery of essential assistance to the Afghan people. Second, stability in Afghanistan cannot be separated from stability in the wider region. We reiterate our call for de-escalation and renewed dialogue between Afghanistan and Pakistan, and we urge all parties to avoid actions that risk further instability, and call for meaningful action against terrorist groups operating in and out of Afghanistan, along with protection of civilians. Third, Afghanistan faces a worsening humanitarian situation. Large-scale returns, extreme weather, and reductions in international system are placing communities under increasing strain. By excluding women and girls from public life, the Taliban are worsening these pressures and undermining Afghanistan's long-term prosperity. The UK remains steadfast in its commitments to the Afghan people. and continue to provide more than $140 million annually over the next three years in support of essential lifesaving assistance for those most in need. Last year, UK-funded programs reached at least 5 million people, including more than 3 million women and girls, and we remain committed to ensuring that women and girls make up at least half those reached through UK assistance. The international community has been clear about what is required. We again call on the Taliban to engage constructively in the UN-led political process and with the wider international community. Our objective remains an Afghanistan that is stable and prosperous, at peace with its neighbors, and respectful of the rights of all of its peoples. Thank you.
I thank the representative of the United Kingdom. I now give the floor to the representative of Panama.

Thank you, Mr.

President. We thank Ms. Georgette Gagnon, officer in charge of the United Nations Assistance Mission in Afghanistan, and Ms. Nargis Nahand. Thank you both for your important briefings. Five years since the Taliban returned to power, 2.4 million girls remain excluded from secondary education. One in three Afghans, that is 13.8 million people, face food insecurity, while 3.7 million girls under the age of five and 1.2 million pregnant and breastfeeding women face acute malnutrition. The recent detention of women in Herat for supposed violations of the dress code shows that these restrictions remain coupled with coercive measures. Ms. Gagnon was very eloquent in her description of the escalation of these restrictions. The decree adopted in May on the legal separation between married couples strengthens the authority of male guardians over marriage and implicitly permits child marriage. The healthcare system that is already extremely fragile continues to lose capacity. Approximately 150 health centres were closed or suspended their operations between January and June due to a lack of funding. In addition to this, there is a contradiction that is difficult to justify. For more than a year, Afghan women who work for the United Nations remain prevented from accessing their workplaces. Part of the personnel whose job it is to contribute to the international response, remain hostage in their own homes. Behind these figures are decisions, and behind these decisions there are responsibilities and consequences. What we are seeing, therefore, are not isolated occurrences, but rather a systematic exclusion of women, which weakens the capacity of society to respond to crises. While humanitarian needs persist, the humanitarian response plan for 2026 is only funded to the tune of 29.9%. Nevertheless, Mr. President, the international community has not abandoned Afghanistan. In June, this Council renewed for one year the mandate of UNAMA. preserving its essential functions and requesting a strategic review. In parallel, both the Council as well as UNAMA have kept communication channels open with Afghan civil society and with humanitarian organizations who continue to work in extraordinarily difficult conditions. These exchanges have also allowed us to shed light on the important contribution of Afghan women to their communities and to the economy of the country as entrepreneurs, business owners, workers, rights defenders and peacebuilders. Their economic, social and political participation must not only be protected, but also recognized as an essential part of the future of Afghanistan. The Doha process maintains dialogue open and has achieved concrete results in areas such as the private sector and the fight against narcotics, and these need to be underscored. In this regard, for Panama, it's essential to keep these channels of dialogue open with the de facto authorities. Experience shows that the challenges that Afghanistan faces require sustained dialogue, trust, confidence and spaces where gradual progress can be made, that enable cooperation and support to be brought about. And that's why we continue to support interactions that are based on principles and focused on concrete results for the Afghan population. Particularly relevant is the Islamabad Declaration adopted in July by the Organization for Islamic Cooperation, whose member states stated the restrictions imposed by the Taliban were incompatible with Islamic values and called for eliminating barriers to education, as well as the work and public participation of women and girls. The OIC, furthermore, is one of the multiple channels for communication that remain open. There are still also serious concerns over the presence and activity of terrorist groups in Afghanistan, including ISIL-K and the Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan, the TTP, and that's why the decisive action of the authorities is required in order to achieve control over this. Panama reiterates that Afghan territory must not be used to threaten the peace and security of any other state. Mr. President, today more than ever, it is the role of the de facto authorities to demonstrate the political commitment required in order to address the grave situation that this country faces. None of this is incompatible with the identity, culture or religion of Afghanistan. It's necessary for the Afghan authorities to assume the responsibilities that are inherent to participation in the international community. For five years, the international community has kept the doors open to dialogue. It is now for the de facto authorities to show through actions their willingness to move towards these doors. The people of Afghanistan deserve to participate fully in the political, economic and social life of their country and to live in conditions of dignity, security, with their fundamental rights respected. Thank you very much.
Thank you for that statement. I now give the floor to Greece.

President, I would like to thank Deputy Special Representative Georgette Gagnon and Ms. Nargis Nehan for their remarks. Mr. President, Last month marked five years since the fall of Kabul and the return of the Taliban to power. What has the international community witnessed in the years since? The human rights of the Afghan people are being systematically violated, most notably through the law on the propagation of virtue and prevention of vice. Women's and minority rights are completely disregarded, with women and girls excluded from public life and denied access to education and employment. The so-called penal code and the code on judicial separation of spouses have further exacerbated restrictions on women's rights, effectively legitimizing domestic violence and child marriage. On the security front, the Taliban have shown a persistent unwillingness to dismantle terrorist organizations operating within their territory. In view of the above, I would like to make the following three points. First, we reiterate our call on the Taliban to respect and protect the human rights and fundamental freedoms of the Afghan people and to lift all restrictions and oppressive measures against women and girls. Repressals against human rights defenders are deplorable. We condemn arrests and arbitrary detentions, including the incidents in Herat against women protesters in June. We also stress the importance of freedom of expression and pluralistic media, and call for the reversal of all relevant restrictions. Second, the Taliban's relationship with the international community and the United Nations continues to deteriorate significantly. For a year now, Afghan women UN employees have not been allowed to enter their offices, with catastrophic repercussions for the delivery of life-saving assistance to those in need. We call for unhindered access for all United Nations personnel to their places of work. Even more concerning was the arrest and detention by the Taliban of two Afghan staff members of UNAMA last August without formal charges. While these employees have since been released, we call for such incidents not to be repeated and for full respect for the privileges and immunities of the United Nations. In this regard, we welcome the appointment of the new SSG for Afghanistan, Ms. Rabab Fatima, and believe that it sends a powerful message to the Taliban regarding the necessity of sustained engagement with the international community and with senior women officials. We reiterate our support for UNAMA and its comprehensive approach, as well as for the Doha process, and we hope that renewed impetus will generate tangible progress. Third, we reiterate the urgency of combating terrorism in Afghanistan, including terrorist activities directed against neighboring countries. The reduction in cross-border clashes is both welcome and necessary for the protection of civilians and the unhindered delivery of humanitarian assistance. The Taliban must ensure that the territory of Afghanistan does not serve as a safe haven for terrorist groups and must step up the fight against all such groups operating inside the country. Mr. President. Taking stock of five years of Taliban rule, the regression is undeniable. The Afghan people cannot afford to lose any more time. The Taliban must engage meaningfully with all relevant stakeholders to facilitate the reintegration of Afghanistan into the international community in full conformity with international obligations regarding human rights, inclusive governance, and counterterrorism.

I thank the representative of Greece for that statement. I will now deliver a statement in my capacity as the representative of France. I'd like to thank Ms. Georgette Gagnon, first and foremost, the AI representative of the Secretary-General, as well as Ms. Nargis Nehan, the founder and executive director of Faragir. They painted a distressing picture of the situation in Afghanistan for us today. In five years, the Taliban transformed Afghanistan into a segregated country. It erected barriers to Afghanistan's development. Restoring the rights of Afghan women is a human, a political, a legal, and a moral obligation, but not only. It is also an essential factor if we are to see an Afghanistan that's internally peaceful, stable, and prosperous. Restrictions on the rights of women and girls are an insurmountable barrier to the country's development. Prohibiting women from studying, from working, deprives the Afghan economy from half of its workers. This policy is particularly disastrous, given that the economy's recovery requires us to place priority attention on those who are de facto leading the country. These restrictions also have negative security consequences. They create a fertile ground for radicalization and terrorism, and this in a region where the threat posed by Daesh, Khorasan, al-Qaeda, and TPP looms large. We call on the Taliban to take the necessary measures to address the situation. Barriers to Women's health care access have serious public health consequences. They push up infant mortality, reduce the life expectancy of Afghan women, and do damage to their mental health. Large-scale restrictions on the rights of half of the population go hand in hand with the exceptional levels of repression hitting half of the population. Ever since the Doha process was launched, the Doha process on the future of Afghanistan, France has been participating in this process and we reiterate. that the objective of this process, as the Council said, is a stable and peaceful Afghanistan, an Afghanistan which can meet the needs of its population. Now, this objective cannot be reached without women, nor without inclusive political dialogue involving all of the parties involved, including political opponents, civil society, and minorities. And it goes without saying, women as well. The Council has issued clear demands of the Taliban ever since Resolution 2593 was adopted in 2021. It called on the Taliban to allow safe and unfettered humanitarian access, guarantee inclusive governance, to combat terrorism, to combat drug trafficking, and to respect fundamental rights, in particular those of women. The international community has given the Taliban a seat at the negotiating table in Doha. The international community listened to the Taliban's requests. It's now up to them to listen to ours. It's up to them to lift the obstacles they themselves placed on the path to Afghanistan's development, as well as obstacles to Afghanistan's reintegration in the international community. Last but not least, France welcomes the appointment of the new SRS-G, Ms. Rabab Fatima. We reiterate our support to UNAMA and other agencies present on the ground. France calls on the Taliban to cease hindering these agencies' activities at a time when roughly half of Afghanistan's population is in critical need of humanitarian assistance. The ban on female Afghan employees accessing UN premises, which has lasted for over a year, is unacceptable. This Council must ensure that the missions it mandates are in a position to fulfil their functions in full respect with the UN Charter. By way of conclusion, I'd like to say that France remains mobilised in support of Afghanistan. For decades, we've constantly, we've never stopped, in fact, providing humanitarian assistance. according to the principle of for and by women, and working to ensure respect for fundamental rights. The fight against impunity, against rights violations, is a priority for France. This is why we supported the Human Rights Council setting up an international mechanism to document the most serious crimes being committed in Afghanistan. France will continue to stand in solidarity with Afghans, men and women alike. We'll continue to stand shoulder to shoulder with them. I now resume my function as President of the Council, I now give the floor to the representative of Afghanistan.

Mr. President, congratulations on assuming the presidency and thank you for convening today's meeting. We also wish to thank you, thank France and other signatories for their strong statement this morning in support and solidarity with Afghan women and girls, as well as we extend our appreciation to the previous presidency of the Council under Danish mission for the strong statement issued on the fifth anniversary of illegitimate rule of Taliban last month for the supporting Afghan people. I also would like to express our thanks and appreciation to DS/RS G, Georgette Gagnon, for her comprehensive briefing and UNAMOS continued work under difficult circumstances and our warm congratulations to the appointment of Special Representative Rabab Fatima. And also we would like to thank Ms. Nargis Nahon for her touching and insightful briefing. As we just marked the 25th anniversary of the terrorist attacks of 11 September 2001, we honor the memory of all those who lost their precious lives, as well as the Afghans and international partners who made the ultimate sacrifice in the fight against terrorism. Last month also marked five years since the Taliban seized power by force, long enough to judge the situation by actions and outcomes, not promises. Despite sustained international and UN engagement, Afghanistan's humanitarian, human rights, political, and security crisis continue to deepen. The Council has taken important steps. Resolution 2615 established a humanitarian exemption. Resolution 2679 mandated an independent assessment for a more coherent international approach. And resolution 2721 called for a UN special envoy to advance its recommendations, including a political process. Yet, the Taliban have continued to disregard the legitimate demands of Afghan people and repeated calls of the international community. Nationwide armed conflict has declined, but the absence of a large-scale war should not be mistaken for sustainable peace. Armed opposition has become increasingly visible in several parts of Afghanistan, particularly in the northern and northeastern provinces, including Badakhshan. It is also important to note that current Afghan armed opposition groups, unlike Taliban, have generally not resorted to suicide attacks or indiscriminate IED targeting civilians. The Secretary-General's report made clear that beneath apparent stability, serious risks continue to accumulate. Mr. President, five issues require particular attention. First, Afghanistan faces a profound crisis of political legitimacy and governance. Five years on, there is still no inclusive political system, no accepted constitutional framework, and no accountable institution through which Afghans can influence decisions affecting their lives. Political parties remain banned, political figures face restrictions, including house arrest, and meaningful political dialogue continues to be rejected. Power remains highly centralized. Even those often described as moderate or dissatisfied Taliban figures in Kabul have been unable or unwilling to meaningfully challenge policies imposed by the leadership. Control of territory is not political legitimacy. Legitimacy cannot be built through force, discrimination, and exclusion. Nor should claims of improved governance obscure credible reports of bribery, extortion, abuse of authority, and interference in humanitarian assistance in the absence of independent oversight. Second, the systematic exclusion of women and girls remains the clearest evidence of the Taliban's violation of their commitments and of our collective failure. UNESCO estimates that 2.4 million Afghan girls remain excluded from secondary education. Afghanistan remains the only country in the world where women and girls are formally denied education beyond the primary level. Women continue to face severe restrictions on employment, movement, and participation in public life. Afghan women work for the United Nations remain barred from UN premises, while restrictions on female humanitarian workers undermine assistance delivery. The Taliban have also expanded religious madrassas as an alternative to formal education, raising concerns among Afghans about radicalization and extremism. This is not only a women's rights crisis, it is a national crisis affecting Afghanistan's economy, health, education, development, and long-term stability. No political process can claim legitimacy while women are excluded from decisions about their country's future. We urge all member states, particularly countries of the Islamic world, to remain clear and united. The denial of the fundamental rights of Afghan women and girls cannot be justified in the name of religion, tradition, or culture, as the Taliban have sought to do. Engagement must never become acceptance of institutionalized discrimination. Third, the broader human rights situation remains deeply troubling. Between May and July alone, UNAMA documented 12 killings, 13 arbitrary arrests and detentions, and the three cases of torture or ill treatment involving former officials and former security personnel, despite the proclaimed general amnesty. Journalists continue to face detention, media outlets are suspended or censored, corporal punishment is carried out, and civic space remains severely restricted. We are also deeply concerned by increasing pressure on Hazara and Shia communities, including the detention of religious and community figures, interference with religious observances, discrimination, and the appropriation of land and property. Reports of targeted killings and reprisals continue. In recent days, a former judge was reportedly shot dead in Kabul, two former security personnel were reportedly tortured and beheaded in Takhar, and other killings were reported in Kabul, Uruzgan, and Herat. Every such case requires a credible and independent investigation. The Taliban cannot credibly claim to provide security while people can be killed, detained, tortured, or disappeared without accountability. Fourth, terrorism remains a serious threat to Afghanistan, the region, and beyond. The Secretary-General notes continuing concern over terrorist groups operating from Afghanistan, while the Security Council's monitoring team has reported the presence of more than 20 terrorist groups. Taliban assurances that Afghan territory will not be used or threaten other countries must therefore be judged by measurable and verifiable action, not statements. Afghanistan must never again become a safe haven, recruitment center, or operational base for international terrorism. At the same time, legitimate counterterrorism concerns cannot justify military actions that kill Afghan civilians or violate Afghanistan's territorial integrity. Such concerns can only be addressed sustainably through legitimate, accountable, and effective governance. Afghanistan must not become a battlefield for the security disputes of others. Fifth, the humanitarian and economic crisis remains severe. 23 million people need humanitarian assistance, and 13.8 million face acute food insecurity, while the 2026 humanitarian response plan is only 30% funded. Nearly 1.15 million Afghans returned between January and August this year, many involuntarily, following approximately 3 million returns in 2025 into communities already struggling with unemployment, food insecurity, and weak services. We call on all States to respect non-refoulement. Returns must be voluntary, safe and dignified, with special protection for women at risk, human rights defenders, journalists, former officials and former security personnel. We also appeal to donors, do not abandon the Afghan people because of the policies of those who rule them. Humanitarian assistance must continue, but it cannot permanently substitute for functioning economy, legitimate institutions, and responsible governance. Mr. President, five years of experience also requires an honest assessment of international policy. Isolation alone has not produced change, neither has engagement without clear political objectives. This false choice between isolation and normalization must end. What is needed is principled, coordinated, and outcome-oriented engagement with a clear political destination, legitimate, representative, and accountable governance through a genuine intra-Afghan political process. This Council has repeatedly supported such an approach. We believe time has come to implement the recommendations of the independent assessment, including the appointment of a UN special envoy, and we hope the ongoing strategic review will strengthen UNAMOS political role. But no durable outcome can emerge from engagement between the Taliban and foreign governments alone. Afghanistan is broader than the Taliban. we therefore reiterate our call for a genuinely Afghan-led and Afghan-owned political process, facilitated by the United Nations and supported by regional and international partners, meaningfully including Afghan women, civil society, political and democratic forces, youth, ethnic and religious communities, and other credible Afghan stakeholders. Afghanistan must be Afghans must be participants, not spectators, in decisions about their future. Last month, our mission conducted voluntary and anonymous consultations with Afghans inside the country and abroad. Among respondents inside Afghanistan, 86% said that their lives had deteriorated over the past five years. 76% identified legitimate, inclusive, and accountable governance as a priority. 71% called for the UN support for an inclusive political process, and nearly two-thirds emphasized meaningful Afghan participation in national dialogue. Their message is clear. Afghans want rights, representation, accountable institutions, education, and opportunity, and above all, a meaningful role in determining how their country is governed. Mr. President, we welcome We welcome the renewal of UNAMIR's mandate and look forward to the strategic review. Its humanitarian and human rights roles are essential, but so is its political role. UNAMIR should help create the conditions for a political solution. I therefore urge the Council and the broader international community to maintain five priorities: a cohesive international approach; protection of the rights and meaningful participation of women and girls, support for a genuine Afghan-led political process, sustained attention to terrorism, human rights, and accountability, and continued humanitarian assistance and protection for vulnerable Afghans. Afghanistan must not be abandoned to an indefinite status quo, not only because of what is at stake for the Afghan people, but also because of the implications for international peace and security. Afghans are not asking the international community to choose their leaders. They are asking for the right to choose their own future. Thank you, Madam President.
I thank the representative of Afghanistan for their statement. I now give the floor to the representative of the Islamic Republic of Iran.

In the name of God, the most compassionate, the most merciful. Thank you, Madam President, for convening this important meeting. At the outset, we congratulate Ms. Rabab Fatima on her appointment as the Special Representative of the Secretary-General and head of UNAMA. and we share every success in discharging this important responsibility. We look forward to further constructive and close cooperation with her. UNAMA plays a vital and indispensable role in assisting the Afghan people, facilitating dialogue, coordinating international assistance, and promoting a coherent and coordinated international approach to Afghanistan. We thank the Secretariat and UNAMA for their continued efforts to support the people of Afghanistan. We thank the briefers for their insightful briefings. We take note of the Secretary-General's latest report, which notes some economic stabilization and efforts by the de facto authorities to maintain governance and economic activities. At the same time, the report indicates that Afghanistan continues to face serious challenges, including acute humanitarian and economic needs, restrictions affecting women and girls, and the persistent threat of terrorism. Against this backdrop, I would like to make the following points. First, five years after the de facto authorities assumed power, The significant reduction in armed conflict and violence across much of Afghanistan and the relative improvement in the security situation are important gains. That must be preserved. However, the terrorist threat remains. ISIL-K and other extremist groups operating in Afghanistan and the region continue to pose a serious threat to Afghanistan and neighboring countries. Addressing this threat requires sustained and strengthened regional cooperation. The Afghan authorities have a responsibility to prevent their territory from being used to plan or carry out terrorist acts against neighboring countries. while the international community and countries of the region should support Afghanistan in strengthening its counterterrorism capacities. Second, the significant reduction in opium cultivation is also an important achievement with positive global implications. However, as highlighted in the report, the economic impact on rural communities remain severe. Sustained investment in alternative livelihoods, rural development, and market access is therefore essential to ensure that these gains are durable. Third, the humanitarian and economic situation remains deeply concerning. Declining external assistance, financial and banking constraints, Limited investment and return of Afghan nationals have placed additional pressure on the country's economy and public services. As noted in the report, the 2026 Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan remains severely underfunded, with only 29.9% funded. Humanitarian assistance must therefore be provided on the basis of need and without politicization. Access to food, medicines, healthcare, and other necessities must not be affected by political considerations. Practical arrangements should also be pursued to facilitate Afghanistan's access to its financial resources and assets. so that these resources can support the Afghan people and essential economic and public services. In the meantime, sustainable recovery requires greater focus on trade, investment, employment, and economic infrastructure. Fourth, as a neighboring country, the Islamic Republic of Iran closely follows developments in Afghanistan. Our long-standing historical, cultural, and human ties, and the direct implications for regional peace and stability, underscore the importance of sustained engagement and cooperation. Iran has consistently pursued a practical and neighborly approach. Despite decades of sanctions and economic pressures, And having recently suffered from the U.S. act of aggression and maritime blockade, Iran has hosted millions of Afghan nationals and provided them with access to education, healthcare, and employment opportunities. Iran has also continued to expand economic cooperation with Afghanistan in trade, transit, energy, railway, and agriculture. The further development of trade and transit, including through the capacities of the port of Chabahar and facilitation for Afghan traders, can provide Afghanistan with greater access to regional and international markets. Fifth, continued international engagement with the de facto authorities remains indispensable to advancing stability and addressing Afghanistan's challenges. constructive and principled engagement is also the most effective means of encouraging progress in the protection of human rights, including the rights of women and girls and members of ethnic and religious communities. The Secretary General's report underscores the importance of a comprehensive approach based on principled and pragmatic engagement. Constructive dialogue remains essential to addressing humanitarian, economic, counter-narcotics, and governance-related challenges. Finally, the Islamic Republic of Iran reiterates its support for continued dialogue and cooperation among Afghanistan, the countries of the region, and the international community. and stands ready to further contribute to regional and bilateral efforts in supporting Afghanistan's stability and sustainable development. I thank you, Mr. President.
I thank the representative of the Islamic Republic of Iran for his statement, and I give the floor to the representative of Kazakhstan.

Mr. President, I congratulate France on assuming the presidency of the Council and wish every success during this very busy month. I thank Ms. Rogette Ganon and Nargis Nehan for their valuable insights. We also welcome the appointment of Ms. Rabab Fatima as Special Representative of the Secretary-General and head of UNAMA, and look forward to working closely with her as she assumes her duties. Kazakhstan strongly supports UNAMA's central role and the UN-led Doha process. Five years after the Taliban's return to power, we believe that principled and pragmatic engagement with the de facto authorities remains the most viable path forward. Engagement should not be equated with recognition, but isolation cannot offer a sustainable solution either. We listened very attentively to all the statements and deeply share expressed concerns in the present situation. But the question is what we can do with it. Our immediate priority must remain the well-being of the Afghan people. Most recently, in June, KazAid, together with relevant government agencies, delivered nearly 319 tons of humanitarian assistance to Afghanistan, accompanied by a medical mission of Kazakh doctors providing direct care and professional training. We are also investing in longer-term food security and livelihoods through the Islamic Organization for Food Security, headquartered in Astana, Kazakhstan and its partners recently supported 400 Afghan farmers in Balkh and Jowjan provinces with improved seeds, fertilizers, and climate-smart agricultural training, contributing to sustainable livelihoods and alternatives to illicit cultivation. Mr. President, humanitarian assistance, while indispensable, cannot provide a long-term solution. The next phase of international engagement should gradually move from managing humanitarian dependency towards enabling economic self-reliance. The scale of the challenge is clear. UNDP estimates that three in four Afghans remain unable to meet their basic needs, while economic growth remains insufficient to improve living standards. According to UNDP and UNHCR, more than 6 million Afghans have returned since 2023, placing immense additional pressure on jobs, services, and host communities. This reinforces the need to create jobs, strengthen the private sector, restore functioning financial channels, and expand trade and investment. Kazakhstan is putting this approach into practice. In June 2026, a high-level Kazakh delegation visited Afghanistan, where the annual Kazakh-Afghanistan Business Forum brought together more than 50 Kazakh companies. During the visit, Kazakhstan opened its second trade house in Afghanistan, this time in Kabul, following the establishment of the first one in Herat in 2024. We therefore attach particular importance to Afghanistan's integration into regional economic networks connecting Central Asia, Afghanistan, and South Asia. This year, we hosted the Regional Contact Group of Central Asian countries on Afghanistan in Astana, as well as a meeting of special representatives of Central Asia and the European Union in Almaty, with a strong focus on regional connectivity and economic cooperation. The UN Regional Centre for SDGs for Central Asia and Afghanistan in Almaty provides an important new instrument to advance this agenda. We look forward to close cooperation between the Centre and the UNAMA on sustainable development, connectivity and capacity building. At the same time, there cannot be sustainable recovery without the meaningful participation of Afghan women and girls. Kazakhstan remains concerned by restrictions of their education and employment. Our longstanding educational programs for Afghan youth, including women, reflect our conviction that investing in human capital is essential for Afghanistan's future. We also remain vigilant regarding terrorism and narcotics and believe that progress in countering the threats must be reinforced through sustainable economic alternatives. Kazakhstan will remain a reliable partner of UNAMA and the Afghan people in building a peaceful, stable, inclusive, and economically self-reliant Afghanistan increasingly connected to the wider region. I thank you.
I thank the representative of Kazakhstan for his statements, and I give the floor to the representative of India.

Mr. President, I congratulate France on taking over the presidency of the Council for this month, and thank you for giving me the floor. I thank Ms. Georgia Gagnon, Head of Mission, Deputy SRSG Political for Afghanistan, for briefing this meeting. We also note the briefings by civil society. As contiguous neighbors, the relationship between Indians and Afghans is older than modern maps and boundaries. The roads from Kabul to the plains of Hindustan were not only trade routes, but also corridors of ideas and knowledge, of belief and faith. Over the centuries, empires have risen and receded across these lands, but the thread of friendship and kinship between the Afghan and the Indian has not been broken. It is this spirit that guides my country's policy towards this nation. We stand in favor of peace, stability, and prosperity that could aid sustainable development of Afghanistan, as evidenced by our participation in the Doha Working Group meetings, our strong bilateral development partnership, and our efforts in regional initiatives. Mr. President, I reiterate Prime Minister Narendra Modi's strong belief that India's shared aspiration for a peaceful and secure Eurasia is also closely linked to peace and stability in Afghanistan. Through more than 500 development partnership projects in all 34 provinces of Afghanistan, India has been contributing to its development. Our commitment to providing humanitarian assistance to the people of Afghanistan will continue. We are working with UN agencies as well as others, such as the Afghan Red Crescent Society, to deliver aid to those who need it the most in Afghanistan. Visits of Afghan ministers to India over the last few months have enabled bilateral consultations to discuss cooperation and humanitarian assistance, development projects, healthcare, food security, capacity building, counter-narcotics, sports, education, trade, travel, and connectivity for the welfare and development needs of more than 48 million Afghan people who endure pressing deprivation and suffering, as also hostility and profound neglect of the international community over the last five years. The UN Secretary-General's report identifies the crisis of Afghanistan's weak public health system that has seen the closure of 150 health facilities in the first half of this year. We cannot look away from this dire situation and must invest in preventing a humanitarian catastrophe in Afghanistan. In addition to the 33 tons of vaccines and related material that we supplied for supporting the child immunization program in the last quarter, in this reporting period, India has gifted specialized medical equipment, including neonatal and pediatric care devices, cardiograph machines, ventilators, patient monitors, electrocautery equipment, plastic surgery sets, and specialized medical kits to Afghan health authorities. This was also supplemented by another 17 tons of essential medicines and medical consumables that have reached Kabul to augment the healthcare services. India continues to support development projects in Afghanistan, particularly in the healthcare sector, including the construction of maternity clinics with a view to strengthening medical infrastructure and improving access to essential healthcare services for the Afghan people. We are also discussing pharmaceutical trade, availability of quality and affordable medicines, drug regulation, quality standards, and regulatory cooperation with Afghan agencies. In the area of agriculture, we are discussing agricultural research, quality seeds, irrigation, horticulture, livestock, food processing, and capacity building. Let us recognize, Mr. President, what the World Drug Report 2026 of the UN Office on Drugs and Crime states. Opium poppy cultivation and production in Afghanistan has remained at historically low levels since Afghan authorities banned narcotics in 2022. We believe that forging closer cooperation with agricultural research institutes will aid the Afghan authorities in their commitment to move Afghans away from cultivation of crops that had been aiding the global drug syndicates and help in the global counter-narcotics effort. In partnership with the UN Office on Drugs and Crime, India has provided 68 tons of medical supplies and 34 tons of social support items for the rehabilitation of drug addicts. We urge member states to support this effort. Mr. President, since August 2021, my country has supplied more than 50,000 tons of wheat, over 450 tons of medicines and vaccines, as well as 40,000 liters of pesticides to Afghanistan. We have provided humanitarian assistance and critical care items in the face of disasters such as earthquakes. However, we realize that moving towards economic self-dependence is extremely important for our Afghan brothers and sisters. We have been having discussions on enhancing bilateral trade, facilitating Afghan exports to India and strengthening B2B linkages. India has emerged as a major destination for Afghan exports. And we remain committed to further increasing bilateral trade in support of Afghanistan's economic development. In this regard, India continues to provide tariff-free access to Afghan goods, facilitate trade through the dedicated India-Afghanistan air freight corridor, and issue gratis long-term business visas to Afghan traders. We strongly condemn the trade and transit terror inflicted on Afghanistan in violation of UN declarations on landlocked developing countries, the WTO norms, provisions of the UN Charter and international law, and the tenets of basic human compassion. We also reiterate our deep concern at the humanitarian plight of the Afghan returnees. The Secretary-General's report mentions that in 2025, 2.9 million Afghans were returned, and until 22 August of this year, another 1.15 million Afghans were returned, most of which were involuntary. A forcible return of this nature that is neither safe nor dignified of over 3 million individuals in any other part of the world would have elicited a political outcry in this Council, urgent provision of large-scale humanitarian support, and efforts to ensure better reintegration and assimilation. That there is no such reaction is a sad reflection on the times. We reaffirm that returns must be voluntary, they must be safe, and they must be dignified. and reintegration should receive sustained international support. To this end, India is cooperating with the UN agencies and the Afghan authorities to make provisions for housing, for food, and other essential items to ease the immense pain and hardship the returnees are suffering. To support the shelter and rehabilitation needs of Afghan returnees, India, in July 2026, gifted family tents to the Afghan Ministry of Refugees and Repatriation. In the field of education, our scholarship and fellowship schemes for Afghan students have great uptake. Since 2023, more than 3,000 students have got these opportunities, including 1,000 Afghan women. Another 1,000 scholarships are being offered in the current academic year to Afghan students to pursue bachelor's and master's degree courses in Indian universities. India also continues to provide financial and logistical support to Afghan self-help groups led by women. We reiterate our position that human rights cannot be advanced in isolation from security, development, and economic opportunity. Progress of Afghan society requires principled, practical, and sustained engagement. India supports provision of greater opportunities to all Afghans in all spheres of human endeavor, including for Afghan women. Mr. President, last week, we honored the memory of those taken mercilessly away by the scourge of terrorism 25 years ago in this very city. Earlier this month, the Council members visited the site of this horrible tragedy. May the memory of these victims always remain a motivation to not only fight against all such individuals who are the worst of humanity, but also those who aid, abet, finance, and support these crimes. The international community supported the global campaign to counter terrorism in the wake of 9/11. Let us not forget, however, that al-Qaeda's terror ecosystem established its strategic depth beyond Afghanistan through its affiliates. The leaders of Al-Qaeda who conceived and directed these 9/11 attacks did not escape justice in the wilderness of some ungoverned frontier. Osama bin Laden, who ordered and financed the plot, was tracked down and killed in a fortified compound within a settled, guarded community under Operation Neptune Spear. Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, the principal architect of the operation, was found sheltering in an ordinary residential house. Ramzi bin al-Shibh, who coordinated the hijacker cell after being denied a visa to join them, was sheltering in an urban center. Senior al-Qaeda operative Walid bin Attash, who helped select and prepare several hijackers, was likewise captured separately. Mustafa Ahmad al-Hawsawi, a key financial and logistical facilitator of the 9/11 operation, was captured under similar circumstances. In each case, these were not fugitives hiding in caves or badlands. They were men who had for long evaded detection. Draining this swamp that provided an enabling environment for such monsters of humankind to prosper is very important. The same permissive environment that sheltered the architects of 9/11 has in the years since continued to provide space, support, and impunity to affiliates of Al-Qaeda, such as Lashkar-e-Taiba and Jaish-e-Mohammed, and their like, acquiring different identities to escape this Council sanctions framework and whose leadership and terror training infrastructure have been shielded from consequence. The international community must join hands to address the continuity of such sanctuary in order to ensure that more such individuals are not thrust upon any country or its citizens, and no one loses family and loved ones. India underscores the continued relevance, Mr. President, of UNAMA's mandate and reaffirms its unwavering support to the mission at this critical juncture as it works to advance peace and stability in Afghanistan. We convey our warm wishes to its incoming head, Ambassador Rabab Fatima, as she prepares to assume this important responsibility. Mr. President, once again, we reemphasize the importance of incentivizing positive actions. We cannot firewall 48 million people suffering deprivation and immense hardship out of our collective conscience and expect that there will be no consequences. There is a lot of misery in this world, but the case of Afghanistan is especially dire. And we must recognize its new reality and change our collective approach, much like we have done in other similar situations. The UN and international community must widen its policy toolkit to include positive inducements and nudges as well, so that one day, a young Afghan girl or a boy can also proudly say that the world helped them when it was needed. Afghanistan is also the world's collective responsibility, and this council has an important role to play in discharging it. A beginning can be made with the Council addressing issues that are under its direct mandate. I thank you, Mr. President.

I thank the representative of India for his statement. There are no more names inscribed on the list of speakers. I now invite Council members to informal consultations to continue our discussion on the subject. The meeting is adjourned.
